title: What to watch at the open
text: Friday starts with two big questions. First, NVIDIA: after its CEO resigned on Thursday, will buyers keep coming back, or will selling return? Early trading before the bell was mixed and close to flat. Second, at 8:30 am New York time the government publishes the producer price index, a report on what businesses pay for goods and services. If it comes in hot, bond yields could climb again and growth stocks could feel it. Remember: the first minutes after the open are often the most jumpy of the whole day.

title: NVIDIA could post a sixth losing week in a row
text: NVIDIA closed Thursday at $166.19. It is down about 11% this week, and news reports say a sixth weekly drop in a row would be its longest losing streak since 2012. It sits only 18% of the way up its one year range, very close to its low. Our risk score is 6.0, at the top of the medium zone. Analysts' average price target is about $328, almost double today's price, but targets were set before the CEO news and may come down.

title: A chip machine maker beat expectations
text: Applied Materials builds the machines that factories like TSMC use to make chips. On Thursday after the close it reported sales of about $10.4 billion for the quarter, a bit more than experts expected, and said demand from AI is strong. That is a hint that chip factories keep spending. TSMC closed at $405.49, down 1.9% on Thursday, with a risk score of 4.8.

title: AMD is near the top of its range while NVIDIA is near the bottom
text: Two chip companies, two very different pictures. AMD closed at $585.30, about 84% of the way up its one year range. NVIDIA is about 18% of the way up. Being near a high or a low does not tell you where a stock goes next. It tells you how investors have felt about it over the past year. AMD's risk score is 7.3 (high) and NVIDIA's is 6.0 (medium).

title: Lesson 50: What is the producer price index (PPI)?
text: The producer price index, or PPI, measures how much prices change for things businesses buy and sell, like steel, fuel, trucking or wholesale food. You may already know the consumer price index, which tracks prices shoppers pay at the store. The PPI looks one step earlier in the chain. If a bakery pays more for flour today, it may charge more for bread later. That is why investors watch the PPI: it can be an early warning that inflation is heading up or down. Economists expect a 0.4% rise for October, smaller than September's 1.3% jump. If prices rise faster than expected, the Federal Reserve is more likely to raise interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing cost more and can weigh on stock prices.
